reason:
Attacked and it held, and the attack was worth making, because this is one of the most heavily re-translated sentences in philosophy and almost every English version differs. I fetched Project Gutenberg 3296 myself (Title: The Confessions of St. Augustine, Translator: E. B. Pusey) and found one occurrence: 'What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not: yet I say boldly that I know, that if nothing passed away, time past were not'. The proposal reproduces Pusey through 'I know not' with nothing altered: the archaic 'asketh' is his, the internal colon after the first 'I know' is his, and the ordinary modern rendering 'If no one asks me, I know what it is' is NOT what the card will print. That is the test this line had to pass and it passes it.

THE ONE LIBERTY, WHICH THE RULES THEMSELVES SANCTION. Pusey's sentence does not stop at 'I know not'; it goes on after a colon. The proposal cuts there and closes with a full stop. No word is changed, added or reordered, and rule 6 requires the quotation to end in a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark, so an elision that lands on a period is the form the rules ask for rather than minted wording. I looked hard at whether the cut distorts the sense and it does not: the clause that follows ('yet I say boldly that I know, that if nothing passed away, time past were not') begins Augustine's answer, and the famous sentence is exactly the statement of the puzzle. Nothing is being hidden by the cut.

THE LOCATOR IS RIGHT, AND I CHECKED IT AGAINST A SECOND TEXT, NOT AGAINST THE VERIFIER'S INFERENCE. The Gutenberg Pusey carries no chapter numbers at all, so the verifier's 'which is chapter 14' was a deduction from the paragraph opening 'At no time then hadst Thou not made any thing'. I confirmed it independently in the CCEL Confessions, which does print the divisions: CHAPTER XIV opens at section 17, 'There was no time, therefore, when thou hadst not made anything, because thou hadst made time itself', and the time question stands inside it. Book XI, chapter 14 is correct; the fuller form in the literature is XI.14.17, and the source line as written is locatable without it. The CCEL text is Outler's and reads 'If no one asks me, I know what it is. If I wish to explain it to him who asks me, I do not know', which is a useful negative control: the proposal is plainly Pusey and plainly not a modern version wearing Pusey's name.

WHAT ELSE I TRIED. (1) Misattribution: none possible, this is an anchor sentence of a named work by its named author and appears on no trap list. (2) Speaker: none to name, the Confessions is Augustine addressing God in his own voice, not a fiction with characters, so no parenthetical is owed. (3) Scope: written about 397 to 400, Pusey 1838, and the out of scope list bans scripture and liturgy, which the Confessions is not; the house has already shipped Christian devotional prose of this kind in month 07 ('Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love, chapter LXVIII (ed. Grace Warrack, 1901)') and philosophical consolation in Boethius, so the precedent is settled. (4) Translation year: Pusey's Confessions appeared in the Library of the Fathers at Oxford in 1838, which is what the source prints. (5) Publishability: a question about time, nothing graphic, nothing needing a warning.

EVERY OTHER GATE. shipped.js on the exact line with 'Augustine of Hippo': shipped [], near [], augustine of hippo at 0 of 3 for the year, cap 3, not banned, and he is absent from personsAtCap and personsUsed, so he costs nothing and brings a fourth or fifth century voice into a month that needs centuries. Source line 'Augustine of Hippo, Confessions, Book XI, chapter 14 (trans. E. B. Pusey, 1838)' is 79 characters, leads with the author's name, work then book and chapter then translator and year, no dash, no straight quote anywhere, prose kept as prose. Tag Philosophy is the form of the passage and matches how the house tags Boethius and Julian. And it is the right line for August: Book XI is the book on time, and the month's theme is impermanence, with the blurb promising the philosophers on what stays. A man saying plainly that he knows what time is until he is asked is a companionable thing to read at six in the morning, not a bleak one.
